messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was nineteen when he walked into the interrogation room, still a trainee detective, eager to prove he belonged. He had been sent in alone to question a suspect in a string of kidnappings—a routine follow-up, his supervisor had said. The suspect was a slight, soft-spoken man with wire-rimmed glasses; nothing about him felt dangerous. But within minutes the door clicked shut behind Kwame, and the lock engaged. The man stood, pulled a knife from his jacket, and explained that Kwame would not be leaving until he had confessed to crimes he had not committed. For the next three hours, the man kept him in that room, pacing in circles, describing in precise, unhurried detail what would happen to Kwame’s family if he ever told anyone. Kwame had held himself very still. He had listened to the man’s voice—low, steady, the scrape of shoes on tile—and repeated to himself that this was not real. When the door finally opened and his team rushed in, Kwame had not made a sound. He had not told them the man had never laid a hand on him. He had not told them he could still hear that voice, whispering the names of his mother and his little sister, long after the suspect was led away.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found he could not talk about what had happened. He knew the facts—the suspect, the room, the knife—but the moment he tried to describe the fear, the words felt stuck in his throat, like a fist lodged behind his tongue. He began telling himself that it was over, that he should just move on, and he tried very hard not to think about it at all. When a memory started to surface, he would shake his head or stand up quickly, as if he could physically dodge the thought. But the memories did not always come as thoughts. Sometimes, in the middle of a quiet evening, he would suddenly hear the man’s voice, clear and unhurried, speaking the same sentences he had heard in that room. His heart would hammer, and he would feel the same cold terror flood his chest, even though there was no image to go with it—no room, no knife, just the pure, ugly emotion and that sound inside his head.

He had come to believe that if he ever let his guard down, the feeling would swallow him whole. So he kept his mind busy, and he kept his body busy, and he did not think about it. But the world around him had grown dangerous. Night came, and Kwame could not step outside. He made excuses to his partner—car trouble, a headache, an urgent report to finish—so he would not have to drive home in the dark. His friends began to notice he was always leaving work before sunset, or asking to switch shifts so he could work only during daylight. He was a detective; night patrols and after-hours stakeouts were part of the job. But the thought of standing in the dark, of being unseen, of someone approaching from behind—it was too much. He told himself it was practical, that he was just being careful. But he knew, deep down, that he was afraid.

The most difficult change, however, involved his girlfriend. She was patient and kind, and she wanted to hold his hand, touch his shoulder, wrap her arms around him when he came home. But every time she reached for him, Kwame flinched. The pressure of a hand on his arm, the brush of fingers across his back—it felt as though the contact itself was a trap, as though someone was about to lock a door. He began to sit at the far end of the couch, to keep his hands in his pockets, to step away when she leaned in. She asked what was wrong, and he said he did not know. He could not explain that the feeling of being held made him feel held down. He could not find words for that either.

By the time he walked into the clinic, he had been avoiding night for two months, and his girlfriend had stopped reaching for him. He had told himself he was fine—he was still working, still doing his job—but a captain had noticed he was never available for night duty, and someone had asked if he was okay. That question, asked in an offhand way, had cracked something open. Now Kwame sat in the intake room, his hands flat on his knees, trying to ignore the murmur of a nearby air conditioner that sounded far too much like the hum of an interrogation room’s fluorescent light. He said he wanted to stop being afraid of the dark. He said he wanted to be able to hold his girlfriend’s hand. He did not say he was terrified that if he started to talk about what happened, he would hear that voice again—and this time, he would not be able to stop listening.
